item.title: 2 Chainz Defends Celebrity Perks In Keith Lee Restaurant Debate
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: 2 Chainz defended the perks of fame as Keith Lee stood by restaurant reviews based on how staff treated regular customers.
item.content:encoded:
2 Chainz defended the perks of fame in a disagreement with Keith Lee over restaurant reviews. Lee stood by judging the service a regular customer would get.

The two discussed Lee’s criticism of Esco Restaurant & Tapas on Kirk Franklin’s “Den of Kings.” For the rapper, better treatment came with the work he had put into his career. For the food reviewer, being recognized could change the very experience he was there to assess.

“I’m an entertainer, and obviously we get perks that other people don’t get. That’s just period, my boy,” 2 Chainz said.

He pointed to skipping airport lines as an example. He also questioned whether Lee’s diet as a former athlete shaped his restaurant judgments.

Lee defended sending relatives to place orders without revealing his identity. That allowed him to judge what paying customers could expect, rather than what staff would do for a famous guest.

The dispute involved a business 2 Chainz had built beyond music. He and partner Mychel “Snoop” Dillard had pursued Esco franchises outside Atlanta. Dillard described the concept in 2022: “We’re a restaurant during the day, lounge by night. That’s the culture we create.”

Lee’s stance had already shaped his 2023 Atlanta food trip, when he visited for ONE Music Fest. His complaints went beyond taste to whether people could order food or get a seat.

At Kandi Burruss’ Old Lady Gang, he said his family faced a 90-minute wait, only for staff to offer him a seat as soon as he entered. He left instead.

At The Real Milk and Honey, Lee said relatives were turned away for “deep cleaning” while other people picked up food. He said he again left after a server recognized him and offered service.

His trip also brought praise for Jamaican Jerk Biz, The Dining Experience and Juci Jerk.

item.title: Timbaland Demands Receipts After Ex-Manager Says He Blew His Fortune
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Timbaland's lawyer rejected Gary Marella's overspending account and alleged financial records and an approval email were altered.
item.content:encoded:
Timbaland‘s lawyer answered Gary Marella’s overspending claims Monday, November 2, accusing the producer’s former management team of failing to protect his money and pointing to allegedly altered records.

“Holding someone accountable for the responsibilities they were hired and paid to perform is not shifting blame,” attorney Tynia Coats told Rolling Stone.

Coats and Timbaland alleged that accounting records listed a consultant’s payment as $16,000 even though the consultant received $165,000. They also alleged that emails were changed to suggest Timbaland approved a $250,000 attorney payment when he had approved $100,000.

Coats and Timbaland also called for an accounting of how the producer supposedly spent the money Marella said his team brought in.

The response followed Timbaland’s October 30 lawsuit against Marella and business manager Bruce Seckendorf.

The producer sought $15 million, claiming the men mishandled his finances, collected excess commissions and left his mortgage unpaid. He alleged a 2025 foreclosure notice exposed the problems, which also included unpaid federal taxes and penalties.

Marella disputed the accusations in a statement. He said he began managing Timbaland in 2017, when the producer was already in debt, and helped generate roughly $75 million in business over about nine years.

He blamed Timbaland’s spending for his financial troubles and said the business manager handled the money and paid management commissions.

“The allegation that I paid myself without his knowledge is simply absurd. Managing his finances was not my role,” Marella said.

The suit reached across their business relationship, from commissions on Verzuz payments to the sale of Timbaland’s music catalog. It also accused Marella of mismanaging Beatclub, the marketplace the pair developed to connect music creators with established artists. Both managers were fired in 2025.

Marella had publicly backed the catalog deal when Hipgnosis announced it in October 2019. The acquisition covered a catalog comprising 108 albums and songs. Speaking as Timbaland’s manager at the time, Marella emphasized the buyer’s responsibility to creators.

“It’s important to all creators that their work is in the right hands,” Marella said.

Marella and Seckendorf did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the new allegations.

item.title: Flyysoulja’s New Condo & Car Celebration Ends With Drug Overdose
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Flyysoulja said a drug overdose sent him to a Miami trauma unit before his November 2 release from the hospital.
item.content:encoded:
Flyysoulja said a cocaine, benzodiazepine and Percocet overdose sent him to a Miami trauma unit on October 29. He was released November 2.

The Island Boys rapper, whose real name is Alex Venegas, told TMZ he had stopped using drugs before celebrating a new condo and car. He said he underwent an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. He also described years of addiction.

Percocet combines the opioid oxycodone with acetaminophen, according to its drug label. In its safety warning on opioids and benzodiazepines, the FDA listed risks including “extreme sleepiness, respiratory depression, coma and death.”

The agency said both kinds of drugs affect the central nervous system, which controls most functions of the brain and body.

Flyysoulja had talked about a drug crisis at his home last year. In November 2025, he spoke to fans on Instagram Live after a three-day stay at a mental health center near Miami, as AllHipHop reported at the time.

He said he had taken multiple drugs before damaging his home. He also explained why viewers had seen the episode online: he had been broadcasting without realizing it.

“In the psychosis, I was trying to find something for my hair for hours, and destroyed the home while unknowingly being on Live,” he said.

He also challenged the basis for the police response. He claimed officers had entered the property without proper permission. He further alleged they had mistaken spilled nail polish for blood as they investigated the scene.

At the time, he said his drug use was the problem. He denied he had been suicidal. KaylaThayla, who shares a child with him, said she found out he had been taken in when she went to collect her pets from the house.

His brother and fellow Island Boy Kodiyakredd told fans he would bring Flyysoulja home once the exam was over.

Under the Baker Act, a person can be held for a mental health exam. Florida’s official Baker Act criteria require suspected mental illness, refusal or inability to decide about an exam because of that illness and serious risks of harm without care.

item.title: Cardi B Gives Johns Hopkins Students A ChatGPT Reality Check
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Cardi B urged Johns Hopkins students to pass their classes and leave ChatGPT out of the answers during her Hoptoberfest set.
item.content:encoded:
Cardi B told Johns Hopkins University students to pass their classes without asking ChatGPT for the answers during her Hoptoberfest performance on Sunday, November 1.

“Y’all better pass y’all motherf–kin’ semester,” she told the crowd. “And don’t ask ChatGPT for the answer.”

The rapper took the stage after a last-minute headliner change. Daniel Caesar could no longer perform because of unspecified unforeseen circumstances.

Organizers HOP and LEED announced Cardi’s booking on October 31 and moved the concert from that night to Sunday at 8 p.m. at the Ralph S. O’Connor Center for Recreation & Well-Being.

The original show had sold out on October 21, with hundreds of students on the waitlist. Existing tickets remained valid after the switch. Caesar’s original booking had been announced on October 19, less than two weeks before students learned Cardi would take over.

“When they switched it to Cardi B, I was a little surprised and honestly thought it was fake,” student Bhavya Guru told The Johns Hopkins News-Letter.

As AllHipHop previously reported, the free concert continued a campus tradition that began in 2013. Past Hoptoberfest performers included Khalid in 2025, Rick Ross in 2023 and Desiigner in 2022.

Her campus remarks also followed an earlier complaint about AI content reaching her relatives. In a February 4 post on X, Cardi wrote, “Free my older family members from facebook Ai.”

At Johns Hopkins, one program has already laid out how AI can fit into schoolwork. The Engineering for Professionals program’s student guidance gives instructors several choices about what to allow in class.

The program describes courses that ban AI, courses that allow limited use with disclosure and courses that allow wider use with transparency. Students still have to answer for their own work. That includes checking AI output for errors and bias.

They may also have to say how they used the tools.

That guidance governs the Engineering for Professionals program, where acceptable AI use can vary by course and assignment. Students who do not know what an assignment allows are told to ask their instructor.

“Treat GenAI as a learning partner, not an authority,” the program advises.

item.title: John Legend Reveals No Jay-Z Super Bowl Invite & Backs A Solo Show
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: John Legend said Jay-Z had not called about Super Bowl halftime, but he backed Hov's ability to perform without guests.
item.content:encoded:
John Legend hasn’t received a Super Bowl invitation from Jay-Z, but when he discussed the halftime show, the singer backed Hov’s ability to handle the performance without a single guest.

The Roc Nation artist addressed the subject in an interview with radio host Fadam Got Da Juice. Legend said Jay had not yet contacted him about appearing at the 2027 show.

“I wouldn’t be mad if he said ‘I’m not bringing no guest out,'” Legend said.

He praised the rapper’s catalog as enough to carry halftime on its own. As for his connection to Jay’s company, Legend put it plainly: “I’m part of the family.”

Legend’s place in Jay-Z’s circle extends beyond the stage. AllHipHop reported his management move to Roc Nation earlier this year, after he left Ty Stiklorius and Friends at Work. Jay Brown took over his music management following roughly two decades with his previous team.

Legend was G.O.O.D. Music’s first signed artist, although he never signed directly to Roc-A-Fella Records.

Stiklorius said she would keep working with Legend on business ventures they had developed together. That move put his management in the hands of the company that also helps produce the NFL’s halftime show.

On October 23, Legend and DJ Khaled joined Jay at SoFi Stadium to perform their 2022 collaboration “God Did.” They appeared after Jay finished his main set with “Public Service Announcement,” returning the singer to the same venue that will host the Super Bowl.

That concert was part of Jay’s anniversary run celebrating 30 years of Reasonable Doubt. Scarface and Blue Ivy Carter also appeared during the October 23 show.

The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Jay-Z as the headliner for February 14, 2027, at SoFi in Inglewood, California. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had asked Jay to perform when the timing felt right. Jay initially turned down the idea when Roc Nation partnered with the league in 2019.

The upcoming performance will be Jay’s first time headlining the halftime show. Roc Nation will executive produce the broadcast performance, with Hamish Hamilton directing.

item.title: Will Smith Accused Of Co-Signing Jada’s Death Threat
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Will Smith's former friend Bilaal Salaam sought $3 million from Jada Pinkett Smith over claims of threats and emotional distress.
item.content:encoded:
Bilaal Salaam claims Will Smith backed Jada’s death threat: “You heard what my wife said,” TMZ reports.

Salaam’s original $3 million lawsuit separately accused Jada Pinkett Smith of confronting him at a September 2021 birthday gathering for Will at a movie theater.

He described a friendship with Will that stretched nearly four decades. In his account, Jada arrived with about seven people and warned that he could “end up missing or catch a bullet” if he kept discussing her personal business.

The original California civil complaint also alleged that Jada demanded a nondisclosure agreement and that one of her associates followed Salaam to his car while making more verbal threats.

Salaam claimed the pressure continued as he worked on a memoir. He also accused Jada and her team of retaliating after he declined to help with Will’s public relations following the March 2022 Oscars.

Salaam discussed the Smiths in a 2023 interview, and Jada publicly said she would take legal action. Salaam’s lawsuit claimed damage to his livelihood and reputation, along with emotional distress and health problems.

Those claimed effects have become a major part of the court fight.

Jada asked for a mental examination lasting five to six hours, arguing that Salaam had made his mental condition central to his case.

She asked doctors to assess whether he had the conditions he claimed and, if so, how much they affected him. He claimed fear had pushed him overseas and cost him a long relationship.

He also cited high blood pressure as one of the effects.

The examination was requested by Jada, who has denied his allegations. Salaam had also tried in August to bring Will into the case as a co-defendant and sought to question him under oath.

Jada had already won the dismissal of some of Salaam’s claims under California’s anti-SLAPP process and an order requiring Salaam to pay $32,836 in legal fees. That ruling left him owing money while other parts of the dispute continued.

In June, Salaam said he was homeless and receiving public assistance as he sought relief from the bill. He asked for a reduction or a payment arrangement. By October, the court had declined to ease that obligation.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Diddy’s Ex-Lawyers Say He Owes Over $500K For Just One Lawsuit
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: Diddy's former law firm seeks liens for a claimed $581,893.75 balance tied to his defamation suit against Nexstar and others.
item.content:encoded:
Diddy owes $581,893.75 for one defamation case, his former law firm says, and it wants protection against any money he wins.

Sher Tremonte LLP asked Judge John P. Cronan to set that sum as the unpaid balance in his suit against Nexstar, Ariel Mitchell and Courtney Burgess.

The filings put a price on the firm’s work in that case, beyond the lawyer-exit dispute AllHipHop covered and over numerous claims they were defending him against after Tony Buzbee filed at least 50 lawsuits against the imprisoned mogul.

“Exhibit A reflects that Mr. Combs owes Sher Tremonte $581,893.75 in connection with the work performed in this matter,” Michael Tremonte wrote under oath.

The firm says the judge already let it withdraw and granted a retaining lien, which can protect unpaid fees by holding on to Diddy’s case files, which would make it difficult, but not impossible, for another law firm to take over the case.

Sher Tremonte wants that lien fixed at the stated balance, plus a charging lien aimed at any recovery from the defendants in this suit.

The letter states: “Sher Tremonte further requests that its charging lien…be fixed in the same amount.”

Under New York’s lien law, that protection can reach proceeds from a settlement or judgment in a client’s favor.

Against his estimated fortune, that bill is a drop in the bucket:

A September 2026 report puts his wealth at no less than $400 million.

The claimed balance is about 0.15% of that estimate, though a net worth estimate does not establish how much cash he can access.

Diddy previously disputed the firm’s bills through spokesman Juda Engelmayer, saying he had not approved some charges, as AllHipHop reported in October.

The public declaration says a spreadsheet separates this case’s hours and fees, even where descriptions on the original invoices also mention other matters.

That spreadsheet was submitted under seal, so the public filings do not expose its full billing breakdown to inspect.

This claim concerns the Burgess case alone, rather than Diddy’s total legal bills.

The firm told Judge Cronan it would also provide the underlying invoices under seal if he requests them.

item.title: PlaqueBoyMax Checks Adin Ross Over Blackface Livestream Idea
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: PlaqueBoyMax questioned Adin Ross' respect for Black culture after Ross floated a blackface livestream with Cheesur and Konvy.
item.content:encoded:
PlaqueBoyMax questioned Adin Ross’ respect for Black culture after Ross suggested a blackface livestream with Cheesur and Konvy.

Ross floated the idea on Kick while watching Max and his friends dressed as white men for Halloween. He asked, “we all do blackface, bro?” He also asked his chat whether the idea would bring him hate and argued that he was Jewish rather than white.

During his own November 1 stream, Max connected Ross’ success to the same culture he felt Ross was disrespecting.

“A lot of your success is rooted in Black culture,” he said, before asking, “why don’t you respect Black culture?”

Max also made clear that his criticism did not erase his admiration for Ross as a streamer. He still counted Ross among his streaming GOATs, keeping that praise separate from his objection to the blackface suggestion.

Max’s own work has moved between livestreams and music production. He received a Best Music Streamer nomination for the 2026 Streamer Awards alongside DDG, Bishu and AriAtHome.

The category recognized singing, playing instruments, DJing, producing and composing music. Voting closed on October 31 ahead of the ceremony planned for November 12.

As AllHipHop previously reported, his broadcasts let viewers watch new tracks take shape through the whole live recording process and help choose their names. His music credits also included “Victory Lap” with Fred again.. and Skepta, which earned a 2026 Grammy nomination for Best Dance/Electronic Recording. The Recording Academy listed Max as both an artist and producer on the track.

Ross had faced criticism for making race part of an on-camera cash offer before. In a video uploaded on February 16, 2023, he asked an Omegle stranger to act Black for $100. When the man refused, Ross doubled the proposed payment to $200.

“That’s racist, isn’t it?” the participant asked. Ross replied, “Just act Black for $200!”

After the man did an imitation, Ross accused him of being racist, then said he was joking. Some other callers ended their conversations rather than comply with the request. Viewers also objected to the clip arriving during Black History Month, according to Dexerto.

item.title: Yella Beezy Trial Witness Gets Immunity Then Says “I Made It Up”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: A witness granted immunity in Yella Beezy's murder trial said he fabricated earlier accusations involving the rapper and MO3.
item.content:encoded:
Jose Bodega testified under immunity in Yella Beezy‘s capital murder trial Monday and said he made up his earlier grand jury claims.

“I made it up,” Jose Bodega said, according to FOX 4’s courtroom report.

Bodega, whose legal name is Theodore Thomas, said he had lied when he claimed Yella Beezy and Trapboy Freddy wanted MO3 dead. Judge Chika Anyiam let prosecutors question him as a hostile witness.

Judge Anyiam also told jurors how they could use his past account.

“You may not consider those earlier statements as evidence that the facts stated in them are true,” Judge Anyiam told them.

Jurors could weigh the statements when deciding whether to believe his current testimony, but could not treat them as proof of the rapper’s guilt.

Prosecutor Tommy Adams noted Bodega had stood by his claims for more than 18 months.

Monday’s testimony followed a very different appearance last Thursday. As AllHipHop previously reported, Bodega repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment outside the jury’s presence and declined to answer questions about his grand jury account.

He also would not answer a defense question about whether he had recanted to a detective while accompanied by his attorney. Bodega spoke to the grand jury on February 13, 2025. The record of that session ran 143 pages.

Bodega, Yella Beezy’s childhood friend, had agreed to help in MO3’s murder case as part of a deal in his own federal drug case. Defense expert Julianna Moore discussed that deal at an October 6 hearing.

MO3, whose legal name was Melvin Noble, was killed on November 11, 2020, on Interstate 35E in Dallas. Kewon White chased him on foot with a rifle before shooting him. White was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to life without parole.

Yella Beezy, whose legal name is Markies Conway, pleaded not guilty to capital murder and denied involvement in MO3’s killing. Prosecutors alleged he paid White $40,000 to carry out the shooting.

His lawyers disputed that money trail. Defense attorney Toby Shook argued that cash linked to White came from drug activity, challenging the state’s claim that Yella Beezy financed the killing.

“They have a theory as to what happened, but that can’t fill in all those gaps,” Shook said during opening statements.

item.title: Druski Lands Multiyear Netflix Deal After Funding His Own Show
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Druski signed a multiyear Netflix deal covering new projects and his online catalog, with Mike Epps joining his first series.
item.content:encoded:
Druski has landed a multiyear Netflix deal that brings his online comedy catalog to the streaming service and sets up new projects through his 4Lifers production company.

The agreement was announced November 2. Netflix will license “Coulda Been Love,” “Coulda Been Daddy” and “Coulda Been Records Auditions,” along with skits. Those projects have drawn more than a billion views combined on YouTube. The pact also covers exclusive original content.

“I’ve built my platform by creating characters and comedy that resonate with people,” Druski said in a statement.

The first series under the agreement, “Collect & Praise,” arrives December 1. Druski plays a pastor with an appetite for money in the semi-scripted comedy. Veteran comedian Mike Epps plays a deacon.

Druski paid for the show himself before Netflix acquired it, Deadline reported. The outlet also reported that the deal covers a fixed number of projects. It is not a traditional overall or first-look agreement.

The new business announcement follows the show’s September tease. On “The Diary Of A CEO,” Druski described Netflix passing on multiple projects before returning with interest in the work he had made.

“Now they want to purchase these shows that we’ve made and do more in the future.”

That interview captured an earlier stage of the talks. The November agreement now includes both a slate of new work and licenses for the shows his audience already knows.

Netflix has also made deals with YouTube creators Mark Rober, Ms. Rachel and Good Mythical Morning, The Verge noted. Druski’s agreement adds his character-based comedy to that push for creators who have built their own online followings.

He has been making deals outside television, too. In October, Druski took an equity stake in Gopuff through a separate multiyear partnership. Its terms include product development, merchandise and distribution for Coulda Been Records and 4Lifers. The value of his stake was not disclosed.

“Gopuff has always been my go-to platform, so partnering together felt like a natural next fit,” he said.

Before his Netflix series arrives, Druski is scheduled to host “Saturday Night Live” on November 7, with The Strokes as the musical guest.
